name: Mugwort
lead: Mugwort is a common name for several aromatic Artemisia species: Artemisia vulgaris in Europe, and A. argyi (Chinese mugwort, ai ye) or A. princeps (Korean ssuk, Japanese yomogi) in East Asia.[1] In appearance-focused circles it matters mainly as a soothing botanical in Korean-style skincare, where extracts are used in toners, essences, sheet masks and creams marketed to calm the look of irritated, redness-prone skin and so give a more even-looking complexion.[1][2]

Outside cosmetics the plant has a long record as food, folk medicine, incense, insect repellent and moxibustion fuel.[1] Its leaves carry essential oils rich in camphor, cineole and thujone, and laboratory studies have reported antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory activity for extracts, which is the usual basis for skincare claims.[1][2]

Mugwort pollen is a leading cause of hay fever and allergic asthma in northern Europe, North America and parts of Asia, and people sensitive to other Asteraceae plants may react to the herb.[1][2] No published human trial has tested mugwort as a skincare ingredient; registered human research involving Artemisia concerns pollen allergy diagnostics and immunotherapy and other Artemisia species for non-skin conditions.[3][4]

chain: Mugwort extract applied in a toner, essence or mask
Marketed as calming irritated, red-looking skin
angle.text: Brands and users describe mugwort products as a way to soothe the look of reactive, blemish-prone or flushed skin, usually as one step in a layered Korean-style routine. The claim rests on traditional use and laboratory findings on the plant's terpenes rather than on skincare trials.

paras: In skincare, mugwort appears as a leaf extract or water in toners, ampoules, cleansers, sheet masks and soothing creams, most often from Korean and Japanese brands that build products around ssuk or yomogi. The positioning is calming: users with sensitive, redness-prone or breakout-prone skin look for it as a gentle step that leaves the complexion looking less irritated.[1][2]

Some consumers also use mugwort teas, baths and compresses at home as part of traditional self-care, drawing on the plant's long folk reputation for itching and skin soreness. Indigenous North American groups made washes and salves from related mugwort species for bruises, itching, sores and eczema, and the Wikipedia article records those uses without describing a cosmetic tradition.[1]

Mugwort has been used since at least the Iron Age as medicine, food and protective herb. It flavoured beer in Iron Age Germany before hops took over, and appears as mucgwyrt in the Anglo-Saxon Nine Herbs Charm recorded in the 10th-century Lacnunga.[1] Medieval Europeans regarded it as protective against evil and fatigue.[1]

In Korea ssuk is eaten in spring soups with clams (ssukguk), steamed with rice flour, and added to rice cakes, teas and pancakes; in Japan yomogi gives colour and flavour to kusa mochi and other sweets, and bundles of yomogi and iris leaves are hung at doorways in some regions to ward off evil.[1] Folk medicine has used mugwort for sleeplessness, menstrual cramps, worms and fevers.[1]

Artemisia princeps is native to China, Japan and Korea; in Japan its young leaves are boiled and pounded into kusa mochi and kusa dango, and in Korea it appears in jeon pancakes, ssuk kimchi, ssukguk soup and rice cakes, with modern ssuk tea, lattes and ice cream [18]. It also features in the Korean Tan'gun myth as one of the foods of medicinal or religious value [18].

In traditional Chinese medicine, aged and pulverised mugwort leaf (moxa), usually from A. argyi, is burned on or near acupuncture points. A review of the mechanism of moxibustion discusses the ancient theory alongside modern research on heat, circulation and immune effects.[7] A randomised trial of mild moxibustion for diarrhoea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome and a randomised placebo-controlled study of an A. argyi extract for functional dyspepsia have been published, both for digestive conditions rather than skin.[5][6] A 2012 Cochrane review found moxibustion did not reduce breech presentation compared with placebo, while calling for better trials.[1]

Moxibustion has a long record in East Asian medicine: Wikipedia describes Bian Que (c. 500 BCE) as its first specialist, and Portuguese missionaries in sixteenth-century Japan were the first Westerners to write about it, calling it 'fire button'. Hermann Buschoff published the first Western book on it in 1674 [16].

Practitioners describe direct moxibustion, in which small cones are burned on the skin, and indirect forms using a moxa stick held near the skin or on an acupuncture needle; a modern self-adhesive version also exists [16]. Practitioners say it warms points to improve circulation and qi flow. Wikipedia notes that most research comes from China and is generally low quality, that a 2023 Cochrane review rated the evidence on breech presentation as moderate certainty, and that reported risks include burns and infection [16].

Artemisia argyi, silvery or Chinese mugwort, is a perennial about a metre tall, native to China, Korea, Mongolia, Japan and the Russian Far East; it is called ai cao or ai ye in Chinese, Chosen yomogi in Japanese and Hwanghae ssuk in Korean [17]. Wikipedia lists traditional Chinese medicine uses including menstrual complaints, asthma and cough, and moxibustion, and notes roughly 96 volatile constituents identified in the leaves, including 1,8-cineole and camphor [17].

Artemisia princeps, Korean and Japanese mugwort, is the species behind most ssuk and yomogi food and is one of the mugwort species burned as moxa [18]. Artemisia vulgaris is the common European mugwort [1].

The essential oil contains camphor, cineole, alpha- and beta-thujone, artemisia ketone, borneol and bornyl acetate, along with phenols, terpenes and other compounds. Composition varies with species, plant part, habitat, harvest season, climate and soil, and thujone content is especially variable.[1]

Preliminary laboratory studies report antimicrobial, antifungal and anti-inflammatory properties for mugwort extracts, attributed to these terpenes.[1][2] Plant essential oils as a class have shown bactericidal activity against food-borne bacteria in microplate assays, but those studies tested many oils and isolated compounds in vitro rather than mugwort on human skin.[8] Related Artemisia species are the source of artemisinin, the antimalarial compound whose derivatives are being studied for cancer and autoimmune disease; that research concerns A. annua, not the mugwort used in skincare.[9][10]

Mugwort pollen is a major allergen, with Art v 1 identified as the principal allergenic protein, and its concentration peaks in the morning hours in season.[1] Reviews of spice and cross-reactive food allergies list mugwort among plants that can provoke reactions in people already sensitised to other pollens or Asteraceae members such as ragweed.[2][11]

Thujone is a neurotoxin at high concentrations; human toxicity from ordinary use is considered weak, but high doses have been linked to seizures and abortive effects, and the Botanical Safety Handbook advises against use in pregnancy without medical supervision.[1][2] Rare minor skin reactions have been reported with moxibustion.[1] A US over-the-counter homeopathic hay fever product listing mugwort pollen carries the label statement that its claims rest on traditional homeopathic practice and are not FDA evaluated.[12]
No studies found on mugwort as a skincare ingredient.

Registered human research involving mugwort is about allergy. A phase 2 study begun in 2014 with 30 participants set out to find the smallest Artemisia vulgaris allergen extract dose that produced a positive skin-prick reaction (NCT01984541), and a phase 2 trial that started in 2026 enrolls 138 people with mugwort pollen-induced allergic rhinitis to test subcutaneous immunotherapy (NCT07563439).[3][4] Studies of other Artemisia species and moxibustion address digestive, malaria and other conditions.[5][6][7]

Mugwort sits at the meeting point of folk tradition, wellness media and K-beauty. Regional and natural-health outlets have run pieces describing it as a plant with medicinal qualities and a distinctive smell, and a 2026 natural-health site article presented it as supporting digestion and skin health.[13][14] Herbalism communities share documentaries and posts presenting mugwort as medicine and magic.[15]
The Linnaean name Artemisia vulgaris dates to 1753 and honours the Greek goddess Artemis, linked in classical tradition to herbs and women's health.[2]

Wikipedia's Artemisia princeps article cites a 2017 laboratory study reporting that an antioxidant A. princeps extract increased expression of the skin-barrier proteins filaggrin and loricrin through the AHR/OVOL1 pathway [18]. Cited by proponents as a plausible basis for barrier-soothing claims, this was a cell-level study and not a trial in people wearing mugwort products [18]. Other laboratory work on A. argyi extracts reported antifungal activity and reduced mutagenicity in bacterial assays [17].

Mugwort is one of the nine plants of the Nine Herbs Charm, an Old English metrical spell recorded in the tenth-century Lacnunga manuscript (British Library Harley MS 585), and the charm includes one of the two clear mentions of Woden in Old English poetry [19]. A 2025 study by folklorist Sara Bonadea George links the charm's mugwort passage to a much later Gotland item from 1875 [19].

lore.intro: Mugwort is discussed in skincare and herbalism circles as a gentle, calming botanical with a long folk history; looksmaxxing forums themselves say little about it.[15]

claims.believers: Korean-style skincare fans and brands describe mugwort toners and masks as soothing for sensitive or reactive skin, citing the plant's traditional use for itching and sores.[1][15]
claims.experts: No published human trial has tested mugwort skincare; laboratory studies report anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial properties of extracts.[1][2]

claims.claim: Mugwort is a broadly healing plant with proven medical uses
claims.believers: Herbalist videos and posts describe it as healing across almost every region of the world and as validated in several medical fields.[15]
claims.experts: Moxibustion trials exist for conditions such as irritable bowel syndrome and dyspepsia, while a Cochrane review found no benefit for breech presentation; the plant is also a common pollen allergen.[1][5][6]

claims.claim: Mugwort is safe because it is natural
claims.believers: Users point to its centuries of use as food and tea in Korea and Japan.[1]
claims.experts: Mugwort contains thujone, a neurotoxin at high concentrations; guidance advises against use in pregnancy, and allergic reactions occur, particularly in people sensitive to Asteraceae.[1][2]

claims.claim: Moxa burning with mugwort treats many conditions
claims.believers: Practitioners say warming acupuncture points with moxa improves circulation and qi flow and treats 'cold' conditions [16].
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes most research is low quality; a 2023 Cochrane review rated breech-presentation evidence as moderate certainty with poor safety reporting; burns and infection are reported risks [16].

card.summary: Artemisia herb used in K-beauty as a calming botanical; folk use is long, skin trials are absent and pollen allergy is common.
card.note: Pollen allergen; thujone content; avoided in pregnancy per herbal safety guidance.

quick.overview:
Mugwort refers to several Artemisia species used in food, folk medicine, moxibustion and, more recently, skincare billed as calming.

No human trials of mugwort skincare were found; evidence cited in sources is traditional use and preliminary lab findings.
quick.mechanism: Extracts contain terpenes such as cineole, camphor and thujone, which preliminary studies associate with antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory activity.
quick.risks: Mugwort pollen is a common allergen and the plant may trigger reactions in people sensitive to Asteraceae. Thujone is a neurotoxin at high concentrations, and herbal safety guidance advises against use in pregnancy.
